Children should use banking, payment, investing, and digital-asset tools only with a parent or trusted adult. No investment or digital asset is guaranteed to increase in value. Publisher, ISBN, website, and contact information to be added before commercial release. Dedication For every child who deserves a fair chance to understand money—and every parent who is willing to learn beside them. The Promise of This Book Every child deserves a clear, joyful path to understanding money, and every parent deserves an invitation to walk that path with them. Money does not grow on trees. Knowledge does. And knowledge grows into wealth.

6 CHAPTER 1 The Day the Tree Chose Them Houston, Texas The crowd roared as a giant screen counted down over Discovery Green in downtown Houston. “Ten!” the crowd shouted. Golden lights flashed across the park. A drone carried a bright sign above the stage: YOUTH INNOVATION CHALLENGE - GRAND PRIZE: $1,000 Alex stared up at it. “One thousand dollars?” Renee smiled. “Now I know why you wanted to come.” “I came for the learning.” “You came for the prize.” “I can do both.” The two best friends moved through rows of youth businesses and inventions. One student had built a robot that sorted cans. Another sold handmade bracelets. A girl their age showed an app that helped families find free meals. “Everybody built something,” Alex said. “And every project began with an idea,” Renee answered. After the event, they walked toward the food trucks. Alex stopped at a picture of loaded fries. “Those look perfect.” “They cost ten dollars,” Renee said.

7 Alex found one dollar and two quarters in his pocket. Renee had three dollars. Together, they had four dollars and twenty- five cents. “This is painful,” Alex said. Nearby, a child asked his father for food. The father checked his wallet and said, “Not today. We have food at home. Wanting something does not mean we can always buy it. We have to choose what our money does.” Renee watched them leave. “Our parents say things like that too.” “They work all day,” Alex said. “Sometimes they are too tired to explain it.” Money moved everywhere around them, but the reasons behind each choice were harder to see. Alex looked at the few dollars in his hand. “Why does money feel simple when you have it and confusing when you do not?” A warm breeze moved through the park. A golden leaf floated between them and landed in Alex’s hand. Words appeared on it: WHAT IS MONEY FOR? Then the words changed: TO SPEND? TO SAVE? TO GROW? TO GIVE? The leaf lifted and floated toward a narrow path behind a row of trees. “That path was not there before,” Renee said. Alex grabbed his bike. “We are following it.” “That is how people disappear in movies.” “It is also how adventures start.”

8 They followed the leaf. With every step, the city grew quieter. The path opened into a clearing where a giant tree stood. Its roots spread like rivers. Its leaves shone green, silver, and gold. A deep voice rose from the roots and branches. “What is money for?” Renee answered first. “To buy things we need.” One branch glowed. “And things we want,” Alex added. Another branch lit up. “To save for later,” Renee said. “To grow,” Alex said. The roots shone brighter. “And what will you do with what you grow?” the tree asked. Renee thought of tired parents and curious children. “Share what we learn.” The whole tree filled with golden light. “Money does not grow on trees,” the voice said. “Knowledge does. And knowledge can grow into wealth.” A golden seed appeared between them. When Alex touched it, images flashed around them: a savings jar, a family budget, a small business, a bank account, a house key, an investment chart, and a parent and child talking at a kitchen table. A tiny golden leaf appeared on each of their palms. “Why did you choose us?” Renee asked.

9 “You asked the first question,” said the tree. “How can money become more than something you spend?” A new branch grew from the trunk. One word appeared on it: VALUE “What does value mean?” Alex asked. “Return when you are ready to find out.” Back in the park, the trail disappeared. The tree had not given them money. It had given them questions. Renee looked at the four dollars and twenty-five cents they still had. “What will you do with yours?” Alex put it back in his pocket. “I do not know yet.” “That sounds like the next question.” They rode home beneath the Houston skyline, knowing the Money Tree had not chosen them because they were rich. It had chosen them because they were ready to learn what money could become. Money Tree Lessons Money is a tool. People can use it to buy, save, grow, give, and build opportunities. New Money Words  Money  Value  Wealth  Choice Renee's Saving Tip Before spending, ask: What else could this money do?

10 Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Do not think only about what money can buy. Think about what it can help build. Money Tree Challenge Ask a parent what money meant in their home growing up and what lesson they wish they had learned earlier. Family Conversation What money lesson do you wish someone had taught you earlier? Quick Review Explain the chapter lesson in your own words. Name one choice the characters made, one risk they faced, and one action you can practice this week. Parent and Caregiver Note Keep the conversation honest and shame-free. Use pretend numbers when family finances are private. Children do not need perfect answers; they need a trusted adult willing to learn beside them.

11 CHAPTER 2 What Is Money, Really? Houston, Texas The next morning, Renee and Alex returned to Discovery Green. The hidden trail was gone. A flyer slid across the grass and stopped at Alex’s shoe. YOUTH MARKET DAY - BUILD IT. SELL IT. LEARN! The event began in two hours. “We should enter,” Alex said. “With what?” Renee asked. They watched children preparing booths. One bored child drew on the back of a receipt while his parent worked. “What if we make activity packs for kids?” Renee said. They used paper, crayons, markers, tape, string, and pencils from their backpacks. They created mazes, drawing pages, and a game called Make a Dollar. Each pack cost about one dollar to make. They priced it at two dollars and called it the Money Tree Fun Pack. At first, no one stopped. Renee opened a sample pack and spread the pages across the table. Alex demonstrated the coin game. Their new sign explained the value clearly: KEEP KIDS BUSY WHILE THEY LEARN - $2 A father bought the first pack. Soon only one remained. A younger boy approached with seventy-five cents. “That is all I have.”

12 Alex offered a trade. The boy could pay the coins and help clean their table after the market. With his mother’s approval, he agreed. After the boy finished the work, a golden leaf landed on the table. “Money is a tool people use to trade value,” it read. The leaf showed people trading apples for bread and baskets for fish. “But what if the person with bread does not want apples?” Alex asked. The words changed. “Money makes trading easier.” The hidden trail appeared. At the tree, Renee and Alex counted ten dollars and seventy- five cents in sales. “We made almost eleven dollars!” Alex said. “We received almost eleven dollars,” Renee corrected. “The supplies cost about six dollars.” They subtracted the cost. “Four dollars and seventy-five cents,” Alex said. “That is our profit.” The tree glowed. “Revenue is what enters. Cost is what the work requires. Profit is what remains.” A branch marked TRADE began to grow. The tree showed them five forms of value: product, service, skill, time, and an idea that solves a problem. “We used all five,” Alex said.

13 They divided the profit. Renee saved her share. Alex wanted to grow his. The Money Tree had not created their money. They had noticed a problem, made a product, taken a risk, and done the work. Money had appeared because value had been exchanged. Money Tree Lessons Money helps people trade value. Revenue minus costs equals profit. New Money Words  Money  Value  Barter  Revenue  Cost  Profit Renee's Saving Tip Replace supply money before spending business income. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Start with a real problem you can solve. Money Tree Challenge Design one safe product or service. List the customer, cost, price, and possible profit. Family Conversation What skill have you used to create value, and who taught it to you?

15 CHAPTER 3 The Want That Felt Like a Need Houston, Texas On Monday, Alex showed Renee a flyer for black-and-gold shoes with glowing soles. They cost one hundred and forty dollars. “I need them,” he said. Renee looked at the clean shoes on his feet. “You want them.” At the Money Tree, a golden leaf showed a family choosing between roof repairs and a new television. The roof was a need. The television was a want. Then it showed a child with holes in their shoes choosing between plain shoes and expensive glowing shoes. “A need is important for health, safety, learning, or daily life,” said the tree. “A want can bring joy, but you can live without it.” Alex admitted his current shoes still fit. The glowing shoes were a want. On the way home, a store sign offered BUY NOW, PAY LATER. The small print included fees and late charges. “Pay later does not mean pay less,” Renee said. Alex decided to wait thirty days and save toward the full price. At home, his father gave him three questions: Do I still want it after waiting? Can I buy it without missing something important? Will I still be happy with the choice later?

16 Alex made three boxes: Needs, Savings, and Shoe Fund. The Money Tree grew a NEEDS AND WANTS branch. Alex still wanted the shoes. But now the want no longer felt like an emergency. Knowing the difference gave him control. Money Tree Lessons Needs come first. Wants are not bad, but they can wait. New Money Words  Need  Want  Fee  Choice Renee's Saving Tip Use a waiting period before buying a want. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip A money plan can include fun without hurting important goals. Money Tree Challenge List five needs and five wants. Choose one want and set a waiting period. Family Conversation What is something you once wanted badly but decided not to buy? 18 CHAPTER 4 Earn It, Don’t Just Ask for It Houston, Texas Alex had eight dollars in his shoe fund and needed a safe way to earn more. While biking through the neighborhood, Renee and Alex saw Mrs. Carter struggling with a crowded garage. She offered them ten dollars each to sort boxes into Keep, Give Away, and Sell piles. They called their parents for permission and began. Alex rushed and made mistakes. He almost placed a box of family photos in the sale pile. Mrs. Carter told him, “Work feels slow when you only think about getting paid. Think about the person you are helping and the result you are creating.” They slowed down and finished well. Mrs. Carter paid each of them ten dollars and added a two-dollar bonus for staying focused and correcting mistakes. She also showed them an old sewing kit. At Renee and Alex’s age, she had learned to sew and used that skill to help her family. At the Money Tree, a new EARNING branch appeared. The tree showed four paths: time, skill, product, and service. “What you earn matters,” the tree said. “How you earn matters too.” At home, Alex divided his twelve dollars. Eight went to his shoe fund, three to savings, and one to spending. His shoe fund reached sixteen dollars.

19 Renee divided her money among saving, a future goal, giving, and spending. They learned that earned money carries proof: their time mattered, their skills mattered, and they could create value again. Money Tree Lessons Useful work can create income through time, effort, skill, products, and services. New Money Words  Earn  Job  Product  Service  Skill  Bonus Renee's Saving Tip Save part of every amount you earn. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Ask what useful thing you can do—not only how to get money. Money Tree Challenge List three safe, adult-approved jobs you could do and the problem each job solves. Family Conversation What skill has helped you earn money? Quick Review Explain the chapter lesson in your own words. Name one choice the characters made, one risk they faced, and one action you can practice this week.

20 Parent and Caregiver Note Keep the conversation honest and shame-free. Use pretend numbers when family finances are private. Children do not need perfect answers; they need a trusted adult willing to learn beside them.

21 CHAPTER 5 Save First, Spend Second Houston, Texas Alex’s money kept disappearing through small purchases: snacks, phone games, trading cards, and drinks. He had spent twenty-three dollars without buying anything large. Renee showed him the problem. “Stop saving whatever is left. Save first.” At the Money Tree, they saw a bucket with a hole. Money entered at the top and leaked out through unplanned spending. Three glowing jars appeared: SPEND, SAVE, and GROW. “Give every dollar a job,” said the tree. “Saving is not what happens after spending. Saving is part of the plan.” Renee brought Alex three jars. He divided twenty-nine dollars among spending, saving, and growing. At the store, he almost used four of his five spending dollars on a sports drink, but realized he already had water. Over the next two weeks, he saved first each time he earned money. He later divided savings into SHOE GOAL and JUST IN CASE. Renee wanted an art class without touching the thirty-five dollars in her drawing-tablet fund. She sold ten custom bookmarks and earned the class money separately. The SAVING branch grew stronger.

22 “A little saved once is helpful,” the tree said. “A little saved often is powerful.” Alex’s shoe fund reached forty-six dollars. The goal no longer felt impossible. It felt like a path made one choice at a time. Money Tree Lessons Saving means keeping money for later. Save first, not last. New Money Words  Save  Goal  Emergency  Emergency savings  Habit Renee's Saving Tip Choose the savings amount before spending. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Keep different goals separate so each dollar has a clear job. Money Tree Challenge Create Spend, Save, and Grow containers or trackers. Plan how to divide your next ten dollars. Family Conversation What is one thing our family is saving for? Quick Review Explain the chapter lesson in your own words. 24 CHAPTER 6 Give Every Dollar a Job Houston, Texas Alex had twenty dollars and eight different jobs for it. Renee told him he needed a budget. At school, Ms. Lewis gave the class sixty dollars to plan a celebration. Students wanted pizza, cupcakes, drinks, balloons, and prizes, but the total reached ninety-five dollars. Renee and Alex asked what the class needed, wanted, and valued most. They chose a sandwich tray, fruit, water, music, and paper decorations. Their plan served more students and totaled exactly sixty dollars. At the Money Tree, glowing tags read FOOD, HOME, SAVING, GIVING, FUN, and GROWING. “Money without a plan can wander,” said the tree. “A budget gives direction.” Income was money coming in. Expenses were money going out. A budget planned both. Alex made a weekly budget for his own twenty dollars: shoe goal, savings, grow, cousin’s gift, and fun. When he wanted a ten-dollar movie ticket, he did not steal from another goal. He earned seven dollars helping Mrs. Carter label yard-sale items. The BUDGETING branch grew. Three tags appeared: PLAN, CHOOSE, and ADJUST. “A budget is a guide, not a cage,” the tree said. “Make each choice on purpose.”

25 Alex went to the movie and still put money toward his emergency savings and shoe goal. A budget was not punishment. It was a map. Money Tree Lessons A budget is a plan for money coming in and going out. New Money Words  Budget  Income  Expense  Category  Limit  Adjust Renee's Saving Tip Put saving in the budget from the beginning. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip A budget sends money toward goals instead of letting it wander. Money Tree Challenge Make a ten-dollar budget. Make sure every dollar has a job. Family Conversation What is one thing our family plans for each month? Quick Review Explain the chapter lesson in your own words. 27 CHAPTER 7 Where Does the Money Go? Houston, Texas Alex kept fifty-eight dollars in an old sneaker. Renee asked what would happen if the shoe was lost, thrown away, or damaged. With Renee’s mother, they visited a Houston credit union. Mr. Brooks explained that financial institutions help people keep, move, track, and sometimes grow money. A checking account was often used for spending. A savings account was used for later. Deposits added money, withdrawals removed it, and the balance showed what remained. Mr. Brooks also taught them to protect debit cards, PINs, passwords, and account information. He showed them a fake message that tried to scare them into clicking a link. The four safety steps were STOP, CHECK, ASK, and REPORT. At the Money Tree, a shield, arrows, and a sprout glowed. A BANKING branch grew. “A tool is useful when you understand how it works,” said the tree. Alex and his father compared youth accounts by fees, interest, minimum balance, access, and safety. They chose an account with no monthly fee and deposited the fifty-eight dollars. Renee also opened a supervised youth savings account for her drawing-tablet goal.

28 Later, Alex received a fake bank email asking for his password. He stopped, checked the official app, asked his father, and reported the scam. The bank account did not make him wise by itself. He still had to track, protect, and choose. Money Tree Lessons Banks and credit unions can help people store, move, track, and protect money. New Money Words  Bank  Credit union  Deposit  Withdrawal  Balance  Interest  PIN  Scam Renee's Saving Tip Compare fees and rules before choosing an account. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Protect account information. Stop, Check, Ask, Report. Money Tree Challenge Practice a bank record with deposits, purchases, and withdrawals. Recalculate the balance each time. Family Conversation How do you keep track of money in an account?

30 CHAPTER 8 Credit Is Borrowed Trust Houston, Texas Alex’s cousin Marcus received a new phone without paying the full price that day. Renee noticed the important word: today. At the Money Tree, the children saw one borrower return a bicycle on time and another return it late and broken. “Credit is borrowed trust,” said the tree. “Debt is money you owe. Interest is the cost of borrowing.” They learned to read an agreement for the amount borrowed, interest rate, due date, payment, fees, and total cost. Marcus’s phone cost eight hundred dollars, but his payments totaled eight hundred forty dollars. Missing a payment would add a fee. At school, Ms. Lewis explained that lenders look at payment history, ability to repay, and risk. A credit report records how borrowed money has been handled. A credit score is a number based on that record. Alex then saw a financing offer for his shoes: twenty dollars now and eight monthly payments. The total was one hundred sixty dollars before late fees. He decided to keep saving instead. The CREDIT branch grew with four leaves: ON TIME, HONESTY, LIMITS, and PLANNING. “Credit lets you use tomorrow’s money today,” said the tree. “Use it only when tomorrow can afford it.”

31 Alex’s shoe fund later reached sixty-eight dollars. He had not turned a want into a bill. Money Tree Lessons Credit is borrowed trust. Debt is money owed. Borrowing has a total cost. New Money Words  Credit  Debt  Borrower  Lender  Interest  Due date  Late fee Renee's Saving Tip Before borrowing for a want, compare it with waiting and saving. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Always calculate the total cost, not only the monthly payment. Money Tree Challenge Compare saving one hundred dollars with a payment plan that totals one hundred ten dollars. Family Conversation What is one rule you follow when using credit? 33 CHAPTER 9 Make Your Money Work Houston, Texas When Alex’s shoe fund reached ninety-two dollars, he began thinking beyond the shoes. At school, Ms. Lewis planted a bean. It needed water, light, care, and time before it could grow more beans. “Investing means putting money into something that may grow in value or produce income over time,” she said. Saving was safer and useful for short-term goals. Investing involved more risk and usually worked better with long-term goals. At the Money Tree, four pots appeared: SAVINGS, BUSINESS, STOCKS, and CRYPTO. The savings plant grew slowly. The business plant grew but bent in a storm. The stock plant moved up and down. The crypto plant rose fast and fell fast. “Some investments change more than others,” said the tree. “Fast growth can bring fast loss. Never confuse possibility with a promise.” A scale balanced RISK and REWARD. A mixed fruit basket taught diversification: do not place every seed in one field. They also saw compounding. One dollar earned growth, and later that growth earned more growth. With their parents, Renee and Alex used a pretend portfolio. Alex chose more growth and risk. Renee chose more safety. Both plans had reasons and spread the risk. Alex kept his shoe money safe because he needed it soon. His separate GROW money was for long-term learning.

34 The INVESTING branch grew with four rules: KNOW THE GOAL, KNOW THE RISK, SPREAD THE SEEDS, and GIVE THEM TIME. Money Tree Lessons Investing may help long-term goals, but all investments include risk. New Money Words  Invest  Risk  Reward  Stock  Dividend  Volatility  Diversification  Compounding Renee's Saving Tip Do not invest money you will need soon. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Know the goal, know the risk, spread the seeds, and give them time. Money Tree Challenge Create a pretend one-hundred-dollar portfolio and explain the risk of each choice. Family Conversation What long-term goal might investing help with? Quick Review Explain the chapter lesson in your own words. Name one choice the characters made, one risk they faced, and one action you can practice this week.

36 CHAPTER 10 Turn an Idea Into a Business Houston, Texas At Discovery Green, Renee and Alex noticed families waiting in long food lines. They imagined sealed snack packs with water, crackers, fruit, and a money puzzle. Their parents helped them check safety and local rules. They could not simply sell food in the park, so Mrs. Carter allowed them to set up at a community yard sale with adult supervision. They compared prices and found each pack cost one dollar and sixty cents. They set the price at three dollars and invested sixteen dollars each in twenty packs. They wrote an agreement: equal startup money and equal profit. At the sale, customers liked the packs. One customer wanted to pay digitally, so the parents helped set up a supervised payment option. They sold fifteen packs at three dollars and three packs at two dollars. Two remaining packs were donated to a family center. Revenue was fifty-one dollars. The cost of the eighteen sold packs was twenty-eight dollars and eighty cents. Profit was twenty-two dollars and twenty cents. They reinvested twelve dollars and split the rest. At the Money Tree, a new ENTREPRENEURSHIP branch grew. Six steps appeared: NOTICE, PLAN, START, SERVE, LEARN, and IMPROVE.

37 The tree also showed a dishonest seller who lost customer trust. “Profit without honesty weakens the roots,” it said. “Your name is part of everything you sell.” Renee and Alex gathered customer feedback and created two price levels. Their small business was becoming a larger idea: fun products that helped families learn money together. Money Tree Lessons A business solves a problem and creates value for a customer. New Money Words  Entrepreneur  Customer  Startup money  Revenue  Profit  Inventory  Reinvest Renee's Saving Tip Keep business money separate from personal money. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Begin with a problem to solve, then test the smallest useful idea. Money Tree Challenge Create a one-page business plan: problem, customer, product, cost, price, safety, and adult help. Family Conversation What business would you have liked to start as a child?

39 CHAPTER 11 When Wealth Grows Roots Houston, Texas After another Market Pack sale, Renee and Alex earned forty- two dollars in profit. They planned to reinvest twenty dollars, then discussed whether the business should give part of what remained. At a community food pantry, Ms. Green explained that the best gift matches a real need. Expired or unlabeled food could not be used. Money sometimes stretched farther because the pantry could buy in bulk. “Good giving does not shame people,” she said. “A gift should respect the person receiving it.” At the Money Tree, the plants around the tree were dry. When the tree shared seeds and water, the garden grew. “A tree that keeps every drop weakens the garden,” the tree said. “Wealth is not only what you keep. Wealth is also what you strengthen.” Four symbols appeared: MONEY, TIME, WORK, and KNOWLEDGE. Renee and Alex donated six dollars, volunteered for one hour, sorted supplies, and made money activity sheets for children. When Alex saw a classmate at the pantry, he did not embarrass him or ask personal questions. He treated him normally and invited him to help sort cereal. The GIVING branch grew. The tree showed help passing from one person to another across many years.

40 “That is legacy,” it said. “What continues after you.” Renee and Alex added a COMMUNITY category to their business: ten cents from every future pack. They would ask what was needed and give with respect. Giving did not erase their own goals. It placed those goals beside something larger. Money Tree Lessons Giving can include money, time, work, and knowledge. Wise giving protects dignity. New Money Words  Giving  Donation  Volunteer  Impact  Community  Legacy Renee's Saving Tip Plan giving so it does not replace basic needs or safety. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Wealth is stronger when it creates opportunity for others. Money Tree Challenge Choose one safe way to give money, time, work, or knowledge this week. Family Conversation Who helped you at an important time, and what kind of help mattered most?

42 CHAPTER 12 Build Something That Lasts Houston, Texas A golden fruit fell from the Money Tree and showed Renee and Alex a family story. A woman worked two jobs, cared for her children, and saved one dollar each week. Her savings helped her take a class and earn more. Years later, one child attended college and another started a repair business. They passed skills and money lessons to their own children. “The first seed may look small,” said the tree. “But the future may grow from it.” The fruit held six seeds: MONEY, PROPERTY, BUSINESS, KNOWLEDGE, VALUES, and OPPORTUNITY. Generational wealth was more than cash. It was safety, ownership, access, knowledge, and the chance for the next person to begin farther ahead. Renee and Alex wrote a mission for their growing project: We help kids and families learn how money works through fun products, real practice, and shared lessons. Their Market Packs could grow into books, games, classroom kits, digital lessons, and safe learning tools. Alex asked his father what their family had passed down. His father named repair skills, trust, discipline, and the hope of giving Alex more choices than he had. Renee’s mother wanted to pass down confidence—the ability to understand money without fear, pressure, or confusion.

43 At school, Renee and Alex drew Future Trees. Roots were habits and values. The trunk was skill and discipline. Branches were goals. Fruit was what those goals could produce. Seeds were what they wanted to pass forward. At the Money Tree, every branch glowed. At the top, the final branch appeared: GENERATIONAL WEALTH “We made it,” Alex said. “You began,” the tree answered. Lessons must become habits. Habits become systems. Systems create opportunity. Opportunity passed forward becomes legacy. A wooden box rose from the roots. Inside was a blank Family Wealth Book with pages for family stories, goals, skills, businesses, property, investments, records, mistakes, and lessons to pass forward. The Money Tree released golden seeds over Houston toward homes, schools, apartments, businesses, and community centers. It had chosen Renee and Alex not because they already knew everything, but because they were willing to learn and willing to share. Weeks later, Alex reached his one-hundred-forty-dollar shoe goal. He found the shoes on sale for one hundred twelve dollars, bought them without debt, and kept twenty-eight dollars. Renee also completed her art class, kept saving, compared models, waited for a discount, and bought her drawing tablet. Her first drawing showed Renee and Alex beneath the golden tree.

44 Money does not grow on trees. Knowledge does. And knowledge grows into wealth. Money Tree Lessons Generational wealth includes money, ownership, knowledge, habits, and opportunity passed forward. New Money Words  Generation  Generational wealth  Ownership  Asset  Legacy  Opportunity Renee's Saving Tip Save for choices, not only things. Alex's Wealth Builder Tip Build ownership and pass forward both assets and knowledge. Money Tree Challenge Draw a Future Tree with roots, trunk, branches, fruit, and seeds. 46 Epilogue The Seed in Your Hands Renee and Alex thought their journey was over, but the Money Tree left one small seed on the ground. “Every great tree begins small,” the tree said. “Knowledge is only the beginning. A lesson practiced becomes a habit. A habit repeated becomes a system. A system protected becomes opportunity. Opportunity shared becomes legacy.” They carried the Family Wealth Book to school and later held a family money night. Parents and children made savings jars, planned small businesses, shared mistakes, spotted scams, and asked questions together. No one needed to be a banker or an expert. They only needed a place to begin. The seed did not grow in the ground. It grew each time a child asked a question and an adult sat down to answer. Your future tree begins with what you plant today. A Letter to Young Readers Money can feel confusing. Sometimes adults do not talk about it because no one taught them either. Begin with one step: save one dollar, make one plan, ask one question, learn one word, solve one problem, or share one lesson. Every good choice is a seed.

47 A Letter to Parents and Caregivers You do not need to be a banker, investor, accountant, or financial expert. You only need to be willing to begin. Say honestly, “No one taught me this either, but we can learn together.” That sentence can change a family. 48 Money Tree Glossary Account: A record of money held by a financial institution. Asset: Something valuable a person or family owns. Balance: The amount of money in an account. Bank: A business that helps people store, move, borrow, and manage money. Barter: Trading one product or service for another without money. Borrow: To receive something with an agreement to return or repay it. Budget: A plan for money coming in and going out. Business: An activity or organization that sells products or services. Cash: Paper bills and coins. Choice: A decision between options. Compounding: When growth may earn more growth over time. Cost: Money needed to make, buy, or use something. Credit: The ability to borrow now and pay later. Cryptocurrency: A digital asset that can change greatly in value and should be explored only with trusted adult guidance. Customer: A person who buys a product or service. Debt: Money that is owed. Deposit: Money placed into an account. Digital wallet: A tool that stores payment information or certain digital assets.

49 Diversification: Spreading money across different investments to reduce risk. Dividend: Money some companies may pay to shareholders. Earn: To receive money for work or value. Emergency savings: Money kept for unexpected needs. Entrepreneur: A person who starts and builds a business. Expense: Money spent. Fee: Money charged for a service or late action. Financial literacy: Understanding how money works and how to make thoughtful choices. Generational wealth: Money, ownership, knowledge, habits, and opportunity passed forward. Income: Money received. Interest: Money earned on savings or paid on borrowed money. Invest: To put money into something with the hope of future growth or income. Legacy: Something meaningful that continues after a person. Need: Something important for health, safety, learning, or daily life. Ownership: Having legal control of something valuable. PIN: A private number used to protect a card or account. Product: Something made or sold. Profit: Money left after costs are paid. Revenue: All money received from sales before costs. Risk: The chance that something may not go as planned.

50 Save: To keep money for later. Scam: A dishonest trick used to steal money or information. Service: Helpful work performed for someone. Stock: An investment representing part ownership in a company. Value: How useful, helpful, or important something is. Volatility: How quickly and strongly a price moves up and down. Want: Something enjoyable that is not required. Wealth: Money, assets, knowledge, ownership, and opportunities built over time.

51 The 30-Day Money Tree Challenge Day 1: Talk about what money means. Day 2: List three needs and three wants. Day 3: Name one useful skill each family member has. Day 4: Track every purchase for one day. Day 5: Find one small spending leak. Day 6: Ask an adult about a first paid job. Day 7: Choose one family money goal. Day 8: Create a savings jar or tracker. Day 9: Give the next dollar received a job. Day 10: Make a ten-dollar budget. Day 11: Choose one want and set a waiting period. Day 12: Compare two prices for the same item. Day 13: Add a small amount to savings. Day 14: Review the family goal. Day 15: Practice Stop, Check, Ask, Report. Day 16: Identify one example of a scam message. Day 17: Explain the difference between debit and credit. Day 18: Calculate the total cost of a pretend loan. Day 19: Create a pretend investment plan. Day 20: Explain diversification with different fruits. Day 21: Talk about one long-term goal. Day 22: Name one problem a small business could solve. Day 23: Create a product or service idea. Day 24: Calculate cost, price, and profit.

52 Day 25: Ask one possible customer for feedback. Day 26: Choose one safe way to help the community. Day 27: Share one money lesson. Day 28: Add a page to the Family Wealth Book. Day 29: Draw a Future Tree. Day 30: Sign the Money Tree Family Pledge.
